extracted.intended_audience: administrators and Title IX coordinators at elementary, secondary, and postsecondary institutions (recipients of Federal funding); policymakers and legal counsel implementing §106.45 grievance processes
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures governing live hearings, cross-examination, evidentiary limits, confidentiality, informal resolution, and special rules for elementary and secondary schools under §106.45 of the Title IX final regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Postsecondary live hearing requirement (§106.45(b)(6)(i))
rubrics_metrics.description: Postsecondary institutions are required to hold live hearings as part of the §106.45 grievance process; a live hearing gives both parties the most meaningful, transparent opportunity to present views, reduces biased decisions, improves accuracy of outcomes, and increases confidence in fairness and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulations intentionally avoid importing comprehensive court rules; hearings are adapted to be applied by layperson officials. The Department views an adversarial adjudication model as better serving fairness, accuracy, and legitimacy for contested facts. Recipients may continue thorough investigations and use existing investigative materials in the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtual hearing authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may conduct live hearings virtually at their discretion, with technology enabling participants simultaneously to see and hear each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows full hearings with parties, witnesses, and other participants appearing remotely. If technology or access issues exist, recipients may grant temporary delays or limited extensions of time frames for good cause (e.g., transportation or troubleshooting technology).

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate-room participation upon request
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon a party's request, parties must be located in separate rooms for the live hearing (not only for cross-examination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shielding provision is intended to protect safety and well-being while preserving live hearing procedures and cross-examination through advisors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recording or transcript of hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must create an audio or audiovisual recording, or transcript, of any live hearing and make that recording or transcript available to the parties for inspection and review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recordings/transcripts aid appeals and reinforce requirements that decision-makers avoid bias. Department was persuaded by commenters to require this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of hearings and identity protections (§106.71(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearings under §106.45(b)(6) are not public; recipients must keep confidential the identity of individuals who report or are involved in a complaint, except as permitted by FERPA, required by law, or necessary to carry out the regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confidentiality exception applies to disclosures permitted by 20 U.S.C. 1232g and 34 CFR part 99, or as required to conduct the hearing or carry out Title IX obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equal-application requirement for additional recipient rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Any additional provisions, rules, or practices a recipient adopts as part of its grievance process other than those required by §106.45 must apply equally to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples recipients may adopt: instruct advisors to conduct questioning respectfully, decide whether to permit opening/closing statements, specify process for objections to relevance of questions/evidence, place reasonable time limitations on hearings, and other rules applied equally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipient discretion on evidentiary rules with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may adopt evidentiary rules (e.g., excluding misleading, assume-fact, cumulative, repetitive, or abusive questions) so long as such rules apply equally and comport with §106.45 requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any additional evidentiary rules must not conflict with obligations to summarize all relevant evidence in investigative reports, evaluate inculpatory and exculpatory evidence, allow parties to gather and present evidence including witnesses, permit relevant cross-examination, and observe rape-shield protections (with two statutory exceptions). Recipients may decide whether/how to limit evidence introduced at hearing that was not gathered/presented prior to hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to gather, inspect, present, and evaluate evidence; investigative report summary
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have the right to gather and present evidence (fact and expert witnesses); recipients must summarize all relevant evidence in the investigative report and evaluate inculpatory and exculpatory evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-makers must be able to evaluate all relevant evidence; investigators' work carries over into the hearing. Even if no party appears, determinations can be reached based on non-statement evidence gathered and presented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to pose relevant cross-examination questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have the right to pose relevant cross-examination questions to other parties and witnesses under the §106.45 hearing procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients cannot adopt rules that exclude relevant cross-examination questions even if the recipient believes the questions assume facts not in evidence or are misleading, except as permitted under other §106.45 provisions (e.g., privilege, duplicative questions). Advisors typically conduct the cross-examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar on requiring privileged information (§106.45(b)(1)(x))
rubrics_metrics.description: The grievance process is barred from requiring, allowing, relying on, or otherwise using questions or evidence that constitute, or seek disclosure of, information protected under a legally recognized privilege.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This protection applies at all stages of the §106.45 grievance process, including investigator evidence gathering, evidence inspection and review, investigative report, and the hearing. It also applies to privileges held by the recipient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of duplicative or repetitive questions as not relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions that are duplicative or repetitive may fairly be deemed not relevant and thus excluded from the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may fairly deem duplicative/repetitive questions irrelevant and exclude them consistent with equal application of rules to both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection against coercion or intimidation of witnesses; right not to participate (§106.71 and general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: No person should coerce or intimidate any witness into participating in a Title IX proceeding; §106.71(a) protects every individual's right not to participate free from retaliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The live hearing requirement does not permit coercion. The regulations specify that lack of participation has the same consequences for complainant and respondent, and recipients must guard against retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary delays / extensions for good cause
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may apply temporary delays or limited extensions of time frames to all phases of a grievance process where good cause exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of good cause include need for parties/witnesses to secure transportation or the need for the recipient to troubleshoot technology to facilitate a virtual hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal resolution processes and voluntary resolution agreements (§106.45(b)(9))
rubrics_metrics.description: Where facts are not contested, the respondent admits responsibility, or both parties wish to resolve without full adjudication, recipients may facilitate an informal resolution (including voluntary resolution agreements) with both parties' written, voluntary consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients may not condition enrollment, employment, or other rights on waiver of investigation/adjudication rights. The Department declines to authorize unilateral waivers of live hearings; participation in mediation or informal resolution must be voluntary for each party.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption and interplay with State APAs
rubrics_metrics.description: To the extent a recipient can comply with both State administrative procedure acts and §106.45, it must do so; where compliance with both is impossible, the Federal regulations preempt conflicting State law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption may not be necessary when State law requires fewer procedures; complying with §106.45 by providing more procedures does not by itself violate State law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design principle: grievance process avoids full court-like procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.45 grievance process intentionally avoids importing comprehensive rules of procedure (including discovery) and rules of evidence that govern civil or criminal trials; procedures are rooted in due process and fairness that layperson recipient officials can apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process focuses on notice, opportunity to be represented, disclosure, ability to call/cross-examine witnesses, access to reasons for decisions, and appeals, but in a form adapted to an educational setting rather than a court trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision-maker impartiality and equal application
rubrics_metrics.description: Decision-makers are expected to serve impartially without bias; adversarial procedures are expected to reduce the likelihood that any bias held by a decision-maker will prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recording/transcript availability and live observation of parties are cited as mechanisms to reduce unconscious stereotypes or generalizations. Recipients must ensure impartiality per §106.45(b)(1)(iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elementary and secondary school option: hearings may be required and written-question alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: For elementary and secondary school recipients, §106.45(b)(6)(ii) allows recipients to require hearings and prescribes a right for parties to submit written questions to other parties and witnesses prior to a determination whether a hearing is held or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This written question process is described as an appropriately fair, flexible, and trauma-informed alternative by some commenters, and is intended to provide due process while accounting for minors' age and maturity. Commenters raised concerns, however, about retraumatization, implementation difficulties, and the need for legal/forensic training in child-interviewing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special considerations for minors and trauma-informed practices
rubrics_metrics.description: When handling complaints involving children, recipients should consider trauma-informed practices, the role of interdisciplinary teams and trained mental health or forensic interviewers, and the potential for retraumatization from multiple interviews or hostile proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters urged that school administrators are not equivalent to forensic interviewers or criminal investigators and that live or written cross-examination may be inappropriate for very young children or students with disabilities; the Department recognized comments but preserved the written-question/hearing flexibility for K-12 recipients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits and burdens related to scheduling, access, and resources
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should account for administrative burdens of live hearings (coordination of parties, advisors, hearing panels, witnesses), limited resources (especially at smaller institutions), and access barriers (remote campuses, unreliable internet) when implementing hearing procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department allows virtual hearings and temporary delays for good cause to mitigate these burdens, but finds that the value of hearings outweighs such burdens as a policy judgment.
